title: Systems of linear ODEs: x′ = Ax (real & complex eigenvalues)
summary: Systems x′ = Ax are solved by eigenvectors: each eigenpair gives a solution e^(λt)v, complex pairs give two real spiralling solutions, and the signs of the real parts decide long-term behaviour. This unit ties linear algebra (Ch 5) directly to differential equations.

lesson.title: Linear systems in normal form; converting higher-order equations

blocks.text: x′(t) = A(t)x(t) + f(t), where x = (x₁, …, xₙ). Homogeneous if f = 0. Here we focus on constant A.

blocks.title: Convert an n-th order equation to a system
items: Set x₁ = y, x₂ = y′, …, xₙ = y⁽ⁿ⁻¹⁾.
Then x₁′ = x₂, …, xₙ₋₁′ = xₙ, and xₙ′ = (the expression from step 1).

blocks.title: Convert to x′ = Ax + f
blocks.prompt: (a) Write y‴ − 4y′ + y = cos t as a first-order system. (b) Write the coupled system x′ = 2x + y, y′ = −x + 4y in matrix form.
steps: (a) y‴ = −y + 4y′ + cos t. With x₁ = y, x₂ = y′, x₃ = y″: x₁′ = x₂, x₂′ = x₃, x₃′ = −x₁ + 4x₂ + cos t.

blocks.text: The characteristic polynomial of the companion matrix equals the characteristic polynomial of the original ODE, so its eigenvalues are the characteristic roots. Systems contain everything from second-order equations.
The bottom row holds the NEGATED lower coefficients (you moved them to the right side): y″ + 3y′ + 2y = 0 gives bottom row (−2, −3).

blocks.title: Coupled second- and first-order equations (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: Write the system x″ + 3x′ − y = 0, y′ = x + 2y as a first-order system u′ = Au.
steps: Unknowns needed: x, x′ (x appears to second order) and y (first order). Let u₁ = x, u₂ = x′, u₃ = y.
u₁′ = u₂; u₂′ = x″ = −3x′ + y = −3u₂ + u₃; u₃′ = y′ = x + 2y = u₁ + 2u₃.

lesson.title: Theory: solution space, Wronskian, fundamental matrix

blocks.name: Existence, uniqueness, dimension
blocks.text: If A(t), f(t) are continuous on I ∋ t₀, the IVP x(t₀) = x₀ has exactly one solution on all of I. The solutions of x′ = Ax form an n-dimensional vector space.

proof.text: Superposition: (c₁x₁ + c₂x₂)′ = A(c₁x₁ + c₂x₂). The map x ↦ x(t₀) is a linear bijection onto ℝⁿ (existence + uniqueness).

blocks.text: For solutions x₁, …, xₙ: W(t) = det[x₁(t) ⋯ xₙ(t)]. If W ≠ 0 they form a fundamental set; X(t) = [x₁ ⋯ xₙ] is a fundamental matrix, with X′ = AX. General solution x = X(t)c; for an IVP, c = X(t₀)⁻¹x₀.

blocks.name: All-or-nothing
blocks.text: For solutions of one system x′ = A(t)x, W(t) is either never zero or identically zero on I.

proof.text: If W(t₀) = 0, some nontrivial combination Σcᵢxᵢ vanishes at t₀. It is a solution with zero initial value, so by uniqueness it is the zero solution for all t: the set is dependent.

blocks.title: Verify solutions and compute the Wronskian
blocks.prompt: Show x₁ = e⁴ᵗ(3, 2) and x₂ = e⁻ᵗ(1, −1) form a fundamental set for x′ = [2 3; 2 1]x.
blocks.answer: Both are solutions and W = −5e³ᵗ ≠ 0: fundamental matrix X(t) = [3e⁴ᵗ e⁻ᵗ; 2e⁴ᵗ −e⁻ᵗ].

blocks.title: Recover A from a fundamental matrix (exam-hard twist)
blocks.prompt: X(t) = [eᵗ e³ᵗ; eᵗ −e³ᵗ] is a fundamental matrix of x′ = Ax. Find A.
steps: Every fundamental matrix satisfies X′ = AX, so A = X′(t)X(t)⁻¹ (constant). Use t = 0: X(0) = [1 1; 1 −1], X′(0) = [1 3; 1 −3].
Check: A(1, 1) = (1, 1) (eigenvalue 1) and A(1, −1) = (3, −3) (eigenvalue 3), matching the columns eᵗ(1, 1), e³ᵗ(1, −1).

lesson.title: The eigenvalue method: distinct real eigenvalues

blocks.name: Eigen-solutions
blocks.text: x(t) = e^(λt)v (with v ≠ 0 constant) solves x′ = Ax exactly when Av = λv.

proof.text: x′ = λe^(λt)v and Ax = e^(λt)Av. These agree for all t iff Av = λv. The guess e^(λt)v comes from the scalar case y′ = ay ⇒ y = ce^(at): along an eigenvector, A acts like the number λ.

blocks.name: General solution
blocks.text: If A has n linearly independent eigenvectors v₁, …, vₙ (e.g. n distinct eigenvalues), the general solution is x(t) = c₁e^(λ₁t)v₁ + ⋯ + cₙe^(λₙt)vₙ.

proof.text: At t = 0 the Wronskian is det[v₁ ⋯ vₙ] ≠ 0, so these n solutions are a fundamental set.

blocks.title: Recipe
items: Eigenvalues: det(A − λI) = 0 (2×2: λ² − (tr A)λ + det A = 0).

blocks.title: 3×3 with distinct eigenvalues (exam-hard)
steps: Solve c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ + c₃v₃ = (0, 0, 1): third entry c₃ = 1; second c₂ + 1 = 0 ⇒ c₂ = −1; first c₁ − 2 + 1 = 0 ⇒ c₁ = 1.

lesson.title: Repeated eigenvalues with a full eigenspace

blocks.text: A repeated eigenvalue is harmless when its eigenspace has dimension equal to its multiplicity: you still get n independent eigenvectors, and the same formula works with no t·e^(λt) terms. (Symmetric matrices are always like this.)

blocks.title: Repeated eigenvalue, full eigenspace
steps: A − 4I = [−1 −1 −1; −1 −1 −1; −1 −1 −1] has rank 1 ⇒ λ = 4 with a 2-dimensional eigenspace x₁ + x₂ + x₃ = 0, basis (−1, 1, 0), (−1, 0, 1). (Trace 9 = 1 + 4 + 4. ✓)
t = 0: c₁ − c₂ − c₃ = 1, c₁ + c₂ = 2, c₁ + c₃ = 3. Adding all three: 3c₁ = 6 ⇒ c₁ = 2, c₂ = 0, c₃ = 1.

blocks.text: Unlike second-order scalar equations, a repeated eigenvalue does NOT automatically produce t·e^(λt). Only a defective eigenvalue (eigenspace too small, e.g. companion matrices with a double root) needs a generalized eigenvector. Check rank(A − λI).
x′ = λI·x: every vector is an eigenvector, so x(t) = e^(λt)x(0) (straight rays).

If a repeated eigenvalue λ has an eigenspace that is too small (geometric multiplicity < algebraic multiplicity), there are not enough eigen-solutions e^(λt)v. For a 2×2 matrix with a double eigenvalue and only one independent eigenvector v, the missing solution has the form x₂ = e^(λt)(tv + u), where u is a generalized eigenvector: (A − λI)u = v.

blocks.name: Second solution in the defective case
blocks.text: If (A − λI)v = 0 with v ≠ 0 and (A − λI)u = v, then x₂(t) = e^(λt)(tv + u) solves x′ = Ax, and together with x₁ = e^(λt)v it forms a fundamental set.

proof.text: x₂′ = λe^(λt)(tv + u) + e^(λt)v. And Ax₂ = e^(λt)(tAv + Au) = e^(λt)(tλv + λu + v), using Av = λv and Au = λu + v. The two agree.
Independence: at t = 0 the solutions are v and u; u is not a multiple of v (otherwise (A − λI)u would be 0, not v), so W(0) = det[v u] ≠ 0.

blocks.text: This mirrors the repeated-root case of second-order equations: the companion matrix of y″ − 4y′ + 4y = 0 is [0 1; −4 4], with the double eigenvalue 2 and only one eigenvector, and the extra t in te²ᵗ comes from exactly this construction.

blocks.title: Recipe (2×2, double eigenvalue λ, one eigenvector)
items: Check rank(A − λI) = 1 (so the eigenspace is 1-dimensional).
Solve (A − λI)u = v for any one u (it always has solutions).
x = c₁e^(λt)v + c₂e^(λt)(tv + u); fit c₁, c₂ from x(0) = c₁v + c₂u.

blocks.title: Defective eigenvalue IVP
steps: A − 2I = [1 1; −1 −1] has rank 1 ⇒ only one eigenvector, v = (1, −1). Defective.
Solve (A − 2I)u = v: u₁ + u₂ = 1 (second row is the same equation negated) ⇒ take u = (1, 0).

blocks.text: In the defective case, e^(λt)(tv) alone is NOT a solution; you need the +u. And a repeated eigenvalue with a full eigenspace never needs t terms.

blocks.name: Real solutions from a complex pair
blocks.text: If λ = α + iβ (β ≠ 0) with eigenvector v = a + ib, then x₁ = e^(αt)(a cos βt − b sin βt) and x₂ = e^(αt)(a sin βt + b cos βt) are two independent real solutions.

proof.text: e^(λt)v = e^(αt)(cos βt + i sin βt)(a + ib) is a complex solution; its real part is x₁ and imaginary part x₂. Since A is real, A(u + iw) = (u + iw)′ forces Au = u′ and Aw = w′. They are independent because at t = 0 they equal a and b, which are independent (a real dependence would give a real eigenvector for a non-real eigenvalue).

blocks.text: Use ONE eigenvalue of the pair. Taking real parts of the solutions for λ and λ̄ gives the same function twice. Keep the minus sign from i·i = −1.

blocks.title: Complex eigenvalues IVP
blocks.prompt: Solve x′ = [−1 −2; 1 −3]x, x(0) = (2, 3). Describe the trajectories.
steps: x₁ = e⁻²ᵗ(a cos t − b sin t) = e⁻²ᵗ(2 cos t, cos t + sin t); x₂ = e⁻²ᵗ(a sin t + b cos t) = e⁻²ᵗ(2 sin t, sin t − cos t).
x(0) = c₁a + c₂b = (2c₁, c₁ − c₂) = (2, 3) ⇒ c₁ = 1, c₂ = −2.
x = e⁻²ᵗ(2 cos t − 4 sin t, 3 cos t − sin t). α = −2 < 0: spirals into 0. A(1, 0) = (−1, 1) has positive second entry: counterclockwise.
blocks.answer: x(t) = e⁻²ᵗ(2 cos t − 4 sin t, 3 cos t − sin t); stable spiral, counterclockwise

lesson.title: Long-term behaviour and which initial vectors decay

head: Eigenvalues of a 2×2 A
Picture
Behaviour
rows: → 0 only if x(0) lies on the line of the negative eigenvalue's eigenvector

blocks.text: In general: the solution decays iff it has no component along eigenvectors whose eigenvalues have real part ≥ 0. As t → ∞ the term with the largest real part dominates. For 2×2: all solutions → 0 ⇔ tr A < 0 and det A > 0.

blocks.title: Saddle: which initial vectors decay?
blocks.prompt: For x′ = [1 4; 2 −1]x, find the general solution and the initial vectors x(0) for which x(t) → 0.
steps: x → 0 iff c₁ = 0, i.e. x(0) is a multiple of (1, −1).
blocks.answer: x(t) → 0 exactly when x(0) ∈ Span{(1, −1)} (a saddle)

blocks.title: True/False on systems
blocks.prompt: (a) If x₁, x₂ solve x′ = Ax, so does 3x₁ − x₂. (b) If a 3×3 A has a repeated eigenvalue, x′ = Ax cannot have 3 independent eigen-solutions. (c) If all eigenvalues of A have negative real part, every solution → 0. (d) A real 3×3 A can have eigenvalues i, −i, 2i. (e) e^(λt)v solves x′ = Ax whenever Av = λv.
steps: (b) False: [3 −1 −1; −1 3 −1; −1 −1 3] has λ = 4 twice with a 2-dimensional eigenspace.
(c) True: every term has a factor e^(αt) with α < 0.
(d) False: complex eigenvalues come in conjugate pairs; 2i would need −2i.

blocks.text: The origin is an equilibrium of x′ = Ax. It is (asymptotically) stable if every solution tends to 0, and unstable if some solution starting arbitrarily close to 0 moves away. The type of the origin is decided by the eigenvalues, which for a 2×2 matrix are decided by τ = tr A and Δ = det A: λ² − τλ + Δ = 0.

head: Condition on τ = tr A, Δ = det A
Eigenvalues
Portrait
Stability
rows: star node (A = λI) or degenerate node (defective)
stable if τ < 0, unstable if τ > 0

blocks.text: Read a node's picture from the eigenvectors: trajectories approach 0 tangent to the eigenvector of the eigenvalue closer to 0 (the slower direction) and run parallel to the faster one far away. In a saddle the eigenvector lines are the only straight-line trajectories; the stable line belongs to the negative eigenvalue.

blocks.title: Classify portraits
steps: (b) τ = −6, Δ = 8, τ² − 4Δ = 4 > 0 ⇒ real eigenvalues −2, −4 ⇒ stable node.
(c) τ = −4, Δ = 5, τ² − 4Δ = −4 < 0 ⇒ spiral sink (λ = −2 ± i), stable.
(e) τ = 4, Δ = 4, τ² = 4Δ ⇒ repeated λ = 2, defective ⇒ unstable degenerate node.
blocks.answer: (a) saddle (b) stable node (c) stable spiral (d) center (e) unstable degenerate node

blocks.title: Spiral with a parameter (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: For x′ = [a 2; −2 a]x, classify the origin for every real a and give the direction of rotation.
steps: a < 0: spiral sink; a = 0: center; a > 0: spiral source.
Direction: A(1, 0) = (a, −2) has negative second component, so at the positive x-axis the motion is downward: clockwise.
blocks.answer: a < 0 stable spiral, a = 0 center, a > 0 unstable spiral; always clockwise

cards.front: What is a linear system in normal form?

back.text: x′(t) = A(t)x(t) + f(t)
x = (x₁, …, xₙ) is the unknown vector, A(t) an n×n coefficient matrix, f(t) the forcing. Homogeneous if f = 0.
Why: Many coupled quantities (tanks, masses, circuits) change together; matrices let us treat them as one equation.

cards.front: How do you convert an n-th order linear ODE to a first-order system?

back.title: Steps
items: Set x₁ = y, x₂ = y′, …, xₙ = y⁽ⁿ⁻¹⁾.
x₁′ = x₂, …, xₙ₋₁′ = xₙ, and xₙ′ = the expression from step 1.

back.text: Move terms to the right side first: y″ + 3y′ + 2y = 0 has bottom row (−2, −3).

cards.front: Write y″ + 3y′ + 2y = e⁻ᵗ as a first-order system.
How are the eigenvalues of the companion matrix related to the auxiliary equation?

back.text: They are the same: the characteristic polynomial of the companion matrix is the auxiliary polynomial.
Example: y″ − y′ − 6y = 0 → [0 1; 6 1]; det(A − λI) = λ² − λ − 6, roots 3, −2: same as r² − r − 6.
So systems really do include everything from Chapter 4.

cards.front: How do you differentiate and integrate a matrix function? What’s the product rule?

back.text: Entry by entry.
(AB)′ = A′B + AB′   (keep the order)
Example: M = [t² e²ᵗ; sin t 1] → M′ = [2t 2e²ᵗ; cos t 0]; ∫₀¹ M has (1,2) entry (e² − 1)/2.
(A²)′ = A′A + AA′, not 2AA′ in general.

cards.front: Existence–uniqueness and dimension for x′ = A(t)x + f(t)?

back.text: If A(t) and f(t) are continuous on an interval I ∋ t₀, then x(t₀) = x₀ gives exactly one solution, valid on all of I.
The homogeneous solutions form an n-dimensional space: x ↦ x(t₀) is a linear bijection onto ℝⁿ.

cards.front: What are a fundamental solution set and a fundamental matrix? How do you use X(t)?

back.text: Fundamental set: n linearly independent solutions x₁, …, xₙ of x′ = Ax.
Fundamental matrix: X(t) = [x₁ ⋯ xₙ], with X′ = AX.
x = X(t)c,   c = X(t₀)⁻¹x₀
Forced system: x = X(t)c + xₚ.

cards.front: Wronskian for systems: definition and the all-or-nothing property. Why?

back.text: W(t) = det[x₁(t) ⋯ xₙ(t)] = W(t₀)·e^(∫tr A)
For solutions: never 0 (fundamental) or identically 0 (dependent).
Why: If W(t₀) = 0, some nonzero combination vanishes at t₀; by uniqueness it equals the zero solution for all t.
(t, 1) and (t², 2t) have W = t²; they can’t both solve one x′ = A(t)x with A continuous near 0.

cards.front: Check that e³ᵗ(1, 1) and e⁻ᵗ(1, −1) form a fundamental set for x′ = [1 2; 2 1]x, and solve x(0) = (3, 1).

back.title: Steps
items: A(1, 1) = 3(1, 1) and A(1, −1) = −(1, −1): both are solutions.

cards.front: Why does x = e^(λt)v solve x′ = Ax exactly when Av = λv?

back.text: Why: x′ = λe^(λt)v and Ax = e^(λt)Av. Equal for all t ⟺ Av = λv.
x = c₁e^(λ₁t)v₁ + ⋯ + cₙe^(λₙt)vₙ
Valid when v₁, …, vₙ are linearly independent (W(0) = det[v₁ ⋯ vₙ] ≠ 0). Distinct eigenvalues guarantee that.

cards.front: Recipe for x′ = Ax (constant A, real eigenvalues) with x(0) given.

back.title: Steps
items: det(A − λI) = 0; 2×2: λ² − (tr A)λ + det A = 0.
Null space of A − λI for each λ.

back.text: Keep each eigenvector with its own eigenvalue; check Av = λv.
Example: x = −e²ᵗ(1, 1) + e³ᵗ(2, 1).

cards.front: General solution of x′ = [5 −1; 3 1]x, and its long-term behavior.

back.text: Example: For large t (c₂ ≠ 0), x ≈ c₂e⁴ᵗ(1, 1): the largest eigenvalue dominates.

cards.front: Repeated eigenvalue: when is it harmless, and when is it a problem?

back.text: Harmless if the eigenspace dimension (n − rank(A − λI)) equals the multiplicity: still n independent eigenvectors, same formula.
Defective if the eigenspace is too small: you need a generalized eigenvector u with (A − λI)u = v, giving e^(λt)(tv + u) (Nagle 9.8).
Example: Real symmetric matrices are never defective.
Unlike scalar ODEs, a repeated eigenvalue does not automatically produce t·e^(λt).

back.title: Steps
items: A = I + J (J all ones): eigenvalues 4, 1, 1.

cards.front: Real eigenvalues λ₁, λ₂ of a 2×2 system: what do the trajectories look like?

items: Both positive: unstable node; everything nonzero blows up.
Opposite signs: saddle; → 0 only along the negative eigenvector’s line.

back.text: Eigenvalues −3 and 2: not every solution → 0.

cards.front: What are all solutions of x′ = 5I·x (2×2)?

back.text: λ = 5 twice, and every nonzero vector is an eigenvector (the eigenspace is all of ℝ², dimension 2 = multiplicity).
Example: x = e⁵ᵗx(0): straight rays out of the origin.

cards.front: For λ = α + iβ with eigenvector v = a + ib, what are the two real solutions? Why do they work?

back.text:
x₁ = e^(αt)(a cos βt − b sin βt)
x₂ = e^(αt)(a sin βt + b cos βt)
Why: e^(λt)v is a complex solution; A is real, so its real and imaginary parts are each solutions.
Don’t also use λ̄ (it gives the same two); keep the minus sign from i·i = −1.

cards.front: Fast way to get an eigenvector for a complex λ of a 2×2 matrix?

back.text: Rows of A − λI are complex multiples of each other, so use one row (p, q) and take v = (q, −p) or (−q, p).

back.title: Steps
items: x₁ = e⁻ᵗ(2cos t − sin t, cos t), x₂ = e⁻ᵗ(2sin t + cos t, sin t).

back.text: Example: x = e⁻ᵗ(3cos t + sin t, cos t + sin t).

cards.front: Real solutions of x′ = [0 4; −1 0]x. What do orbits look like?

back.text: Example: α = 0: a center; orbits are ellipses x₁²/4 + x₂² = const, period π.

cards.front: How do α and β (λ = α ± iβ) shape the phase portrait? Direction of rotation?

back.text: β sets the rotation speed.
Direction: Compute A(1, 0). Second entry > 0 means counterclockwise.
Example: [1 −5; 1 −3]: A(1, 0) = (1, 1), counterclockwise.

cards.front: Two real solutions of x′ = [3 −2; 4 −1]x; in or out?

back.title: Steps
items: x₁ = eᵗ(cos 2t, cos 2t + sin 2t), x₂ = eᵗ(sin 2t, sin 2t − cos 2t).

back.text: Example: α = 1 > 0: spirals out.

cards.front: True or false: a real 3×3 matrix can have eigenvalues i, −i, 2i.

back.text: False. Conjugating Av = λv shows Av̄ = λ̄v̄: complex eigenvalues of real matrices come in conjugate pairs. 2i would need −2i, making four.
Example: Every real 3×3 matrix has at least one real eigenvalue, e.g. [−1 0 0; 0 0 −3; 0 3 0] has −1, ±3i.

cards.front: Why does each eigenpair (λ, v) give a solution e^(λt)v of x′ = Ax?

back.text: x′ = λe^(λt)v and Ax = e^(λt)Av = λe^(λt)v: equal for all t.

cards.front: For complex λ, how do you get two real solutions, and why are they independent?

back.text: Take real and imaginary parts of e^(λt)v (A real ⇒ each is a solution). At t = 0 they are Re v and Im v, which are independent, so W(0) ≠ 0.

cards.front: All solutions of a 2×2 system → 0 iff?

back.text: Both eigenvalues have negative real part ⇔ tr A < 0 and det A > 0.

solution.title: Solution
items: λ = 3: A − 3I = [1 0 1; 2 0 2; 1 0 1] has rank 1, giving eigenvectors (0,1,0), (−1,0,1); λ = 5 with (1,2,1). Two eigenvectors for the double eigenvalue ⇒ enough for a fundamental set.

solution.text: What it tests: Repeated eigenvalue with a full eigenspace needs no generalized eigenvectors (and no teλt terms).

hard.title: Complex eigenvalues IVP

prompt.text: Find the real general solution of x′ =
x, then solve with x(0) = (1, 1). Describe the trajectories.

hard.answer: x(t) = e²ᵗ(cos t − 3 sin t, cos t + 2 sin t); spirals outward

solution.title: Solution
items: x₁ = e2t(a cos t − b sin t) = e2t(−cos t − sin t, cos t); x₂ = e2t(a sin t + b cos t) = e2t(−sin t + cos t, sin t).
x(t) = e2t(cos t − 3 sin t, cos t + 2 sin t). Real part 2 > 0: trajectories spiral outward (unstable spiral).

solution.text: What it tests: Use one eigenvalue; its real and imaginary parts give both real solutions. Taking real parts of both conjugate solutions gives the same function twice.

hard.title: Companion matrices

prompt.text: (a) Write y‴ − 2y″ − y′ + 2y = 0 as a first-order system x′ = Ax, find the eigenvalues of A, and the general solution y. (b) Write y″ + 3y′ + 2y = sin t as x′ = Bx + f(t).

hard.answer: (a) A = [0 1 0; 0 0 1; −2 1 2], eigenvalues 1, −1, 2, y = c₁eᵗ + c₂e⁻ᵗ + c₃e²ᵗ (b) x′ = [0 1; −2 −3]x + (0, sin t)

solution.text: det(λI − A) = λ³ − 2λ² − λ + 2 = (λ − 1)(λ + 1)(λ − 2) — exactly the characteristic polynomial of the ODE. Eigenvalues 1, −1, 2.
What it tests: The last row of the companion matrix holds the negated lower coefficients (solve for the top derivative first). Its eigenvalues are the characteristic roots.

items: 3. If 3×3 A has a repeated eigenvalue, x′ = Ax cannot have three independent solutions of the form eλtv.
4. If every eigenvalue of A has negative real part, every solution of x′ = Ax tends to 0.
5. Two vector functions whose Wronskian is identically zero on an interval must be linearly dependent there.
1. True. Differentiation and multiplication by A are linear.
3. False. A = [4 0 1; 2 3 2; 1 0 4] has λ = 3 twice with a 2-D eigenspace, giving 3 independent eigen-solutions. (A = I is the extreme case.)
4. True. Every solution is built from eαt(cos, sin)·(polynomial) with α < 0.
5. False. (eᵗ, 0) and (e2t, 0): det = 0 always, but no constant c gives e2t = ceᵗ. (They can’t both solve one system x′ = A(t)x; for actual solutions the implication holds.)

solution.text: What it tests: Eigen-solutions eλtv are the building blocks; what matters is whether you have n independent eigenvectors, not whether eigenvalues repeat.

hard.title: Stability with parameters

prompt.text: x (equivalent to y″ + 2y′ + ky = 0), classify by k: when are eigenvalues real distinct / repeated / complex, and when do all solutions → 0? (b) For x′ =

hard.answer: (a) k < 1 real distinct, k = 1 repeated, k > 1 complex; all → 0 iff k > 0 (b) h < 0 spiral in, h = 0 closed orbits, h > 0 spiral out

solution.title: Solution
items: k < 1: real distinct. Both negative iff √(1−k) < 1 iff k > 0; for k < 0 one is positive (saddle); k = 0 gives λ = 0, −2 (solutions tend to constants).
k = 1: repeated λ = −1 with only one eigenvector (companion matrices are never λI) — a defective case, still decays like te⁻ᵗ.
(b) Eigenvalues h ± 2i. h < 0: spirals into 0; h = 0: closed orbits (ellipses), periodic, bounded; h > 0: spirals outward.

solution.text: What it tests: Real part decides decay/growth; imaginary part decides rotation. For 2×2: trace = sum, det = product of eigenvalues — stable ⇔ trace < 0 and det > 0.

hard.title: Build A from solutions; stable line

prompt.text: Find a 2×2 matrix A for which x′ = Ax has solutions e−t(1, 2) and e3t(1, −1). Which initial conditions lead to solutions that tend to 0?

solution.text: General solution c₁e⁻ᵗ(1,2) + c₂e3t(1,−1) → 0 iff c₂ = 0: x(0) on the line Span{(1, 2)} (saddle).
What it tests: The eigenvector of the negative eigenvalue is the stable line; any component along the other eigenvector eventually dominates.

hard.title: Fundamental matrix IVP

prompt.text: , write a fundamental matrix X(t) for x′ = Ax and solve with x(0) = (0, 1) using x(t) = X(t)X(0)⁻¹x(0).

hard.answer: X(t) = [e²ᵗ e⁻ᵗ; e²ᵗ 2e⁻ᵗ]; x(t) = (e⁻ᵗ − e²ᵗ, 2e⁻ᵗ − e²ᵗ)

solution.text: What it tests: X(t)X(0)⁻¹ = eAt. Columns of X must be independent solutions (Wronskian ≠ 0).

hard.title: Coupled oscillators

prompt.text: Two masses obey x″ = −2x + y, y″ = x − 2y. (a) Write this as a first-order system in ℝ⁴. (b) Solve with x(0) = 1, y(0) = 0, x′(0) = y′(0) = 0, using eigenvectors of K =

hard.answer: x = ½(cos t + cos √3t), y = ½(cos t − cos √3t)

solution.text: (b) Second-order form z″ = Kz. K has eigenvalues −1 ↔ (1,1) and −3 ↔ (1,−1). Try z = f(t)v: f″ = λf ⇒ frequencies 1 and √3.
x = ½(cos t + cos √3t), y = ½(cos t − cos √3t) — a mix of the in-phase and out-of-phase normal modes.
What it tests: Eigenvalue −ω² of K gives angular frequency ω. The ℝ⁴ system has eigenvalues ±i, ±√3i.

keyFacts: nth-order ODE → system: x₁ = y, …, xₙ = y⁽ⁿ⁻¹⁾; companion eigenvalues = characteristic roots.
e^(λt)v solves x′ = Ax ⇔ Av = λv; general solution Σcᵢe^(λᵢt)vᵢ with n independent eigenvectors.
IVP: solve [v₁ ⋯ vₙ]c = x(0); or x = X(t)X(0)⁻¹x(0).
Wronskian det[x₁ ⋯ xₙ]: never 0 (fundamental) or always 0 for solutions.
Repeated eigenvalue with full eigenspace: same formula, no t e^(λt).
λ = α + iβ, v = a + ib: x₁ = e^(αt)(a cos βt − b sin βt), x₂ = e^(αt)(a sin βt + b cos βt).
Decay iff no component along eigenvectors with Re λ ≥ 0; 2×2 stable ⇔ tr < 0, det > 0.

parsons.title: Eigenpairs give solutions
parsons.goal: Prove: if Av = λv, then x(t) = e^(λt)v solves x′ = Ax.
lines: Differentiate: x′(t) = λe^(λt)v, since v is constant.
Since Av = λv, Ax(t) = e^(λt)λv = λe^(λt)v.
So x′(t) = Ax(t) for all t. ∎
distractors: Since Av = λv, v must be a unit vector.

parsons.title: The defective second solution
parsons.goal: Let (A − λI)v = 0 and (A − λI)u = v. Prove x(t) = e^(λt)(tv + u) solves x′ = Ax.
lines: Product rule: x′(t) = λe^(λt)(tv + u) + e^(λt)v.
From the hypotheses, Av = λv and Au = λu + v.
So Ax(t) = e^(λt)(tAv + Au) = e^(λt)(tλv + λu + v).
This equals x′(t), so x solves the system. ∎
distractors: So Ax(t) = λx(t), and x is an eigen-solution.

parsons.title: Wronskian all-or-nothing
parsons.goal: Let x₁, …, xₙ solve x′ = A(t)x on I. Prove: if W(t₀) = 0 for some t₀ ∈ I, then the xᵢ are linearly dependent on I.
lines: W(t₀) = det[x₁(t₀) ⋯ xₙ(t₀)] = 0, so these n vectors are dependent.
Let y(t) = c₁x₁(t) + ⋯ + cₙxₙ(t); by superposition y solves the system with y(t₀) = 0.
The zero function also solves the system with value 0 at t₀.
By uniqueness y(t) = 0 for every t ∈ I, a nontrivial dependence relation on I. ∎
distractors: By existence y(t) = 0 only at t₀.
So W(t) = 0 implies every xᵢ is the zero solution.
